posts.title: Review: Judy - A Look Back
posts.description: Gemma Creagh takes a look back at Jessie Buckley in Judy . The story of Judy unfolds across two defining periods in the life of one of Hollywood’s most enduring stars. In the first timeline, child star Judy Garland is a wide-eyed, impressionable ingénue fighting a losing battle against the repulsively abusive Hollywood system. While in the second, she’s a troubled forty-something wrestling with her demons and struggling to function as a mother and an artist. After one brutal night ferrying her children across LA from hotel to hotel, Judy (Renée Zellweger) is confronted by their father, Sidney Luft (Rufus Sewell). Judy is left with a classic Catch-22: in order to have enough money to care for her kids, she has to take a job in London, but in doing so, she will lose access to her kids. While she weighs up her options, Judy visits the party pad of her eldest, Liza Minnelli (Gemma-Leah Devereux). posts.title: Review: Tin Castle
posts.description: Virginia O'Connor focuses her lens on this second feature by Alexander Murphy. This deft, observational documentary follows the O’Reilly family, comprising Pa’, Lisa, and their 10 young children, who all live together in a mobile home on an isolated road in rural Tipperary. The opening scene features a wide shot of their front door, swinging back and forth as the many family members come and go from their modest home. The keys, left in the door, are carefully framed and serve as a visual motif for the sense of security and trust that underpins family life. This is the O’Reillys’ safe haven in a world that isn’t quite as warm or welcoming. We meet Lisa, the warm, nurturing mother of the brood, as she holds a box of Honey Nut cereal and insists that each of her children has their lunch ready for school. It’s a fitting choice, given that she often uses ‘hunny’ as a term of affection. Meanwhile, Pa’, the family patriarch, is devoted not only to his children but also to his beloved horses.

posts.title: Review: Sense and Sensibility
posts.description: Khushi Jain looks at a film with little sense and very little sensibility. ’Tis the year of Austen, and I am not complaining. I saw Mary Bennet bloom into her own person this spring in BBC’s The Other Bennet Sister , which stars Dónal Finn opposite the delightfully awkward Ella Bruccoleri. And while this miniseries has been renewed for a three-part Christmas special, December will also play host to the much-anticipated Pride and Prejudice , written by Dolly Alderton for Netflix, with Emma Corrin as Elizabeth and James Lowden as the first ginger Darcy. This is all just to say that there is always time, money, and an audience for these adaptations. So let’s talk about the newest instalment in the Austen cinematic tradition, Georgia Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility , or as I’ve been calling it, ‘The Cottage-core Dream Come True’.
